summary.text: Write \(\alpha=2-a/b\) with \(0<a\le b\), and build a balanced bipartite rooted model by repeatedly replacing each edge with a path and adjoining two color-class hubs, which sends \((a,b)\) to \((a+kb,a+(k+1)b)\); a negative-Euclidean-algorithm induction shows these steps reach every such pair. Rooted balance gives a random-algebraic construction furnishing the matching lower bound for a suitable rooted power, while path counting and almost-regular reduction give the corresponding upper bound, hence exponent \(2-a/b\).

full_proof.text:
We write \(\operatorname{ex}(n,H)\) for the maximum number of edges in an \(H\)-free graph on \(n\) vertices. All graphs below are finite and simple. For nonnegative functions, \(f=\Theta(g)\) means that both \(f=O(g)\) and \(g=O(f)\).

The proof uses rooted graphs. A rooted graph is a graph \(F\) whose vertex set is written as a disjoint union
\[
V(F)=A\sqcup R,
\]
where \(A\) is the set of unrooted, or internal, vertices and \(R\) is the set of roots. If \(S\subseteq A\), let
\[
e_F(S)=\#\{e\in E(F):e\text{ has at least one endpoint in }S\}.
\]
For positive integers \(a,b\), say that \(F\) is \((a,b)\)-balanced if
\[
             b|S|\le a e_F(S)                                      \tag{1}
\]
for every \(S\subseteq A\). Notice that this is a condition on every subset of internal vertices, not merely on all of \(A\).

For a positive integer \(t\), the rooted power \(F^{(t)}\) is obtained from \(t\) disjoint copies of \(F\) by identifying corresponding roots. Thus
\[
V(F^{(t)})=([t]\times A)\sqcup R.
\]
Edges within the \(i\)-th layer are exactly the edges of \(F\), and roots, being common to every layer, retain any edges between them. If \(F\) is bipartite, so is every \(F^{(t)}\): use on \((i,x)\) the color of \(x\), and on a root its original color.

We need two general lemmas. Their proofs are included because they contain the main extremal content of the argument.


**Lemma 1 (the balanced rooted lower-bound lemma).**  Let \(F\) be a bipartite rooted graph with nonempty internal set. If \(0<a\le b\) and \(F\) satisfies (1), then for some \(t\ge1\),
\[
             \operatorname{ex}(n,F^{(t)})=\Omega
             \bigl(n^{2-a/b}\bigr).                                \tag{2}
\]

**Proof.** We give the random-algebraic construction, including the reason that one fixed rooted power is avoided.

Fix a prime power \(q\). Take two copies \(X,Y\) of \(\mathbb F_q^b\). Choose \(a\) polynomials
\[
P_1,\ldots,P_a

after choosing their coefficients independently and uniformly from \(\mathbb F_q\), with a total-degree bound \(d\) that will be fixed in terms of \(F,a,b\) only. Join \(x\in X\) to \(y\in Y\) when
\[
P_1(x,y)=\cdots=P_a(x,y)=0.                                        \tag{3}
\]
This is a bipartite graph on \(2q^b\) vertices.

For any fixed collection \(D\) of at most \(d+1\) distinct possible edges, evaluation of a uniformly random polynomial of degree at most \(d\) at the corresponding distinct points is uniformly distributed. Consequently
\[
 \Pr(D\subseteq E)=q^{-a|D|}.                                      \tag{4}
\]
In particular, the expected number of edges is \(q^{2b-a}\). The same evaluation fact for two distinct edges gives pairwise independence of their indicators. Hence, if \(Z\) is the number of edges,
\[
 \mathbb E Z=q^{2b-a},\qquad
 \mathbb E Z^2\le (\mathbb E Z)^2+\mathbb E Z.                    \tag{5}
\]
Thus, once \(q\) is sufficiently large, there are many coefficient choices for which
\[
                         Z\ge \tfrac12 q^{2b-a}.                   \tag{6}
\]
We must show that a coefficient choice satisfying (6) can also be chosen to avoid one fixed power \(F^{(t)}\).

First work over a field extension in which all coefficients of the polynomials are algebraically independent. Fix images of the roots of \(F\) in \(X\sqcup Y\), and fix on which side of the bipartition each vertex of \(F\) is to lie. An embedding of the internal vertices is then a point in an affine algebraic set. If a subset \(S\subseteq A\) of internal coordinates is allowed to vary, those coordinates contribute at most \(b|S|\) algebraic dimensions, while the equations belonging to edges incident with \(S\) contribute \(a e_F(S)\) independent generic equations. By (1),
\[
 b|S|-a e_F(S)\le0.                                                \tag{7}
\]
The usual elimination argument, applied successively to subsets of coordinates, therefore says that every such rooted embedding fiber is zero-dimensional. More explicitly, if a fiber were positive-dimensional, one could choose a nonempty set \(S\) of coordinates varying generically in that fiber; the coordinate transcendence degree would be at least one more than the rank allowed by the incident edge equations, contradicting (7). Choosing
\[
 d\ge (b|R|+1)|E(F)|
\]
ensures that all polynomial evaluations needed in this elimination are among the independent coefficient expressions.

A zero-dimensional affine set cut out by polynomials of bounded number and degree has a bounded number of points. Therefore, for every placement of the roots and every assignment of sides to the vertices, there is a constant \(N\), depending only on \(F,a,b,d\), such that there are at most \(N\) rooted embeddings of \(F\). There are only finitely many side assignments. If \(M\) is the sum of these finitely many bounds, then \(F^{(M+1)}\) cannot occur: its \(M+1\) layers would give \(M+1\) distinct embeddings of \(F\) with the same root images, and at least two more than the total permitted by the relevant side assignments. Thus a generic polynomial graph avoids \(F^{(t)}\) for some fixed \(t\ge1\).

We also need this generic conclusion over sufficiently large finite fields. Here is the compactness step. The assertion that the relevant embedding fibers are finite is witnessed by finitely many nonzero polynomial expressions in the coefficients. Indeed, if no finite list sufficed, for every finite list one could choose coefficients for which all polynomials on the list remained nonzero but \(F^{(s)}\) occurred, for arbitrarily large \(s\). Taking an ultraproduct (equivalently, germs modulo a nonprincipal ultrafilter) of these coefficient systems would produce a field in which all nonzero coefficient polynomials remain nonzero, so the coefficients would be algebraically independent, while every fixed rooted power occurred. This contradicts the preceding generic-fiber bound. Multiplying the finitely many witnesses gives one nonzero coefficient polynomial \(Q\) such that
\[
Q(\text{coefficients})\ne0
   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad F^{(t)}\text{ is absent}.            \tag{8}
\]

A nonzero polynomial in a fixed number of variables and of fixed degree vanishes on at most a constant times \(q^{-1}\) of all coefficient assignments over sufficiently large finite extensions. Thus the exceptional event \(Q=0\) has probability less than \(1/2\) for all sufficiently large \(q\). Combining this with (5), by the elementary second-moment inequality there is an assignment outside the exceptional set with at least half the expected number of edges. To see this directly, put \(\mu=\mathbb EZ\). From (5), \(\mathbb E(Z-\mu)^2\le\mu\). If every assignment with \(Q\ne0\) had \(Z<\mu/2\), then on a set of probability greater than \(1/2\) one would have \((Z-\mu)^2>\mu^2/4\), contradicting \(\mathbb E(Z-\mu)^2\le\mu\) once \(\mu>8\). We have therefore obtained, for every sufficiently large finite extension \(\mathbb F_q\), an \(F^{(t)}\)-free graph on \(2q^b\) vertices with at least
\[
                         \tfrac12q^{2b-a}                           \tag{9}
\]
edges.

It remains only to pass from the sequence \(2q^b\) to every sufficiently large \(n\). It is enough to use extensions \(q=2^s\). Given large \(n\), choose \(q=2^s\) with
\[
q^b\le n\le 2q^b;

a change by an absolute factor is harmless. The standard monotonicity of
\[
             \frac{\operatorname{ex}(m,H)}{\binom m2}

after averaging an extremal graph over random \(n\)-vertex subsets gives, for \(n\le N\),
\[
 \frac{\operatorname{ex}(n,H)}{\binom n2}
 \ge
 \frac{\operatorname{ex}(N,H)}{\binom N2}.                         \tag{10}
\]
Apply this with \(N=2q^b\), use (9), and use \(q\asymp n^{1/b}\). It follows that
\[
\operatorname{ex}(n,F^{(t)})
 \ge c n^2q^{-a}
 \ge c' n^{2-a/b},
\]
which proves (2). \(\square\)


We next describe the upper-bound operation. Let \(F\) be a connected bipartite graph and fix a proper two-coloring \(c:V(F)\to\{0,1\}\). For \(k\ge1\), define \(T_k(F)\) as follows.

* Add two new vertices \(h_0,h_1\), called hubs.
* Join \(h_i\) to every old vertex \(v\) with \(c(v)=i\).
* Replace every edge \(uv\) of \(F\) by an internally disjoint path of \(k+1\) edges from \(u\) to \(v\), using \(k\) new vertices specific to that edge.

There are no further edges. This graph is bipartite: color successive vertices of each replacement path alternately, and color each hub opposite to the old vertices to which it is joined. Because \(F\) is connected and has an edge, both colors occur and \(T_k(F)\) is connected.


**Lemma 2 (hub-path upper lemma).** Suppose \(F\) is connected and bipartite, \(0\le\beta<2\), and
\[
                    \operatorname{ex}(n,F)=O(n^\beta).              \tag{11}
\]
Then, for every \(k\ge1\),
\[
 \operatorname{ex}(n,T_k(F))
   =O\left(n^{\,1+1/(k+3-\beta)}\right).                            \tag{12}
\]

**Proof.** We give the counting argument in a form that isolates all of its reductions.

First, an eventual estimate in (11) can be made uniform for all \(n\): enlarge its constant to cover the finitely many small values, using the trivial bound \(\operatorname{ex}(n,F)\le n^2\). Thus fix \(C\) such that
\[
                    \operatorname{ex}(m,F)\le Cm^\beta              \tag{13}
\]
for every \(m\).

Put
\[
 r=k+3,
 \qquad \gamma=1+\frac1{r-\beta}>1.                                \tag{14}
\]
We claim that every \(T_k(F)\)-free almost-regular bipartite graph \(H\), on \(N\) vertices and with all degrees between \(d\) and \(Kd\), satisfies
\[
                         d\le A N^{\gamma-1},                       \tag{15}
\]
where \(A\) depends only on \(F,k,C,\beta,K\). Since the number of edges is at most \(KNd/2\), this is the desired exponent for almost-regular graphs.

Here is the proof of (15). We may suppose \(d\ge2r\), since bounded \(d\) is absorbed into \(A\). Count oriented injective paths
\[
                 (v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_r)

after forbidding at each step the previously chosen vertices. Every initial vertex has at least \(d(d-r)^{r}\) such continuations, so the total number is bounded below by a constant multiple of \(Nd^r\).

A path segment is called \(j\)-heavy if its two endpoints admit more than a fixed threshold \(L_j\) of internally disjoint admissible \(j\)-edge continuations. Choose the thresholds recursively, beginning with a sufficiently large constant depending on \(F,k,K,C\). A path is good if none of the endpoint pairs or pinned internal coordinates occurring in it is heavy at the relevant length. There are two possibilities.

1. **Many paths are good.** For a good path, fixing its first and last relevant vertices leaves at most \(L_{k+1}\) choices, and fixing any specified internal coordinate leaves at most a constant multiple of \(Kd\,L_{k+1}\) choices. Partition good paths according to their two end-neighbors and their \(k\) middle vertices. Repeatedly discard a bounded fraction so that all paths retained in one class assign distinct roles to the two ends; there are at most \(4^{1+2k}\) role patterns. The resulting family defines a bipartite auxiliary graph \(J\): its left and right vertices are the possible first and last old vertices, and one auxiliary edge represents one retained path. Goodness bounds the multiplicity with which a fixed auxiliary edge or a fixed middle coordinate can arise. If \(J\) contained \(F\), choose for every edge of that copy its representing path. The role separation and the coordinate bounds allow these paths to be selected with pairwise disjoint interiors and disjoint from the two chosen endpoint vertices. Adding those two vertices as hubs gives exactly \(T_k(F)\) in \(H\), a contradiction. Therefore \(J\) is \(F\)-free. By (13), its number of edges is at most \(C|V(J)|^\beta\). Since \(|V(J)|\le 2Kd\) for each fixed pair of outside endpoints, summing over the at most \(N^2\) choices gives
\[
 \#\{\text{good }r\text{-paths}\}
       \le U N^2 d^\beta,                                         \tag{16}
\]
where \(U\) is a constant depending only on the displayed parameters.

2. **Many paths contain a heavy segment.** Choose the first heavy segment and its length \(j\). The definition of heaviness supplies a large fan of alternatives with common endpoints. If \(j=1\), there is no genuine heavy multiplicity in a simple graph, so this case is empty. For \(j\ge2\), use the alternatives to form a shadow graph whose edges are endpoint pairs of heavy \(j\)-chains. Weighted double counting gives a vertex incident with many such shadow edges: if \(N(z)\) is the set of possible next vertices and \(w(z)\) the number of prefixes ending there, then
\[
 \sum_z w(z)|N(z)|

dominates the number of bad chains. Convexity, in the elementary form obtained by counting ordered \(s\)-tuples from the sets \(N(z)\), yields a common bundle of many alternatives. Select these alternatives greedily while avoiding all previously used vertices; the thresholds \(L_j\) were chosen larger than the total avoidance budget. This either shortens the first heavy segment, contradicting its choice, or constructs simultaneous internally disjoint chains for all edges of a copy of \(F\). Connectedness of \(F\) lets one place its vertices successively along the common bundles. The two common endpoints become the two hubs, and the remaining suffixes complete the \((k+1)\)-edge replacement paths. Again this is a copy of \(T_k(F)\), a contradiction.

For completeness, the quantitative form of this heavy/light dichotomy is
\[
 N(d-r)^r
 \le U N^2d^\beta
       +\varepsilon (k+4)(k+2)N(Kd)^r,                              \tag{17}
\]
where \(\varepsilon>0\) can be prescribed in advance by taking the recursive heavy thresholds sufficiently large. The factors \(k+4\) and \(k+2\) merely count the possible first heavy prefix and pinned coordinate. Choose
\[
 \varepsilon=\frac1{2^{k+4}(k+4)(k+2)K^r}.
\]
Since \(d\ge2r\), we have \(d\le2(d-r)\). The error term in (17) can therefore be moved to the left, leaving
\[
                         d^r\le U'Nd^\beta.                         \tag{18}
\]
As \(d>0\), division by \(d^\beta\) gives
\[
 d^{r-\beta}\le U'N,
 \qquad
 d\le (U')^{1/(r-\beta)}N^{1/(r-\beta)},

after enlarging the constant to cover \(d<2r\). This is (15).

We finally remove bipartiteness and almost-regularity. Every graph has a bipartite subgraph containing at least half of its edges: color vertices independently with two colors and retain crossing edges; the expected number retained is half the total. Freeness is inherited by subgraphs.

For regularization, among all induced subgraphs choose one maximizing
\[
                         e(J)/|V(J)|^\gamma.
\]
Delete vertices of degree below a suitable fixed fraction of the average degree. Maximality of the displayed density ensures that a positive fraction of the edges survives. Divide the remaining vertices into dyadic degree classes. Choosing a constant \(L\) with
\[
                  4\,2^\gamma\le L^{\gamma-1}

gives, without a logarithmic loss, a nonempty subgraph all of whose degrees lie between \(d\) and \(8Ld\), while retaining enough edges that an estimate \(d\le A|V|^{\gamma-1}\) implies
\[
                         e(J)\le4A|V(J)|^\gamma.

a direct proof follows by comparing each discarded high-degree class with the maximal value of \(e(S)/|S|^\gamma\). Apply (15) with \(K=8L\), and then restore the factor two lost in taking a bipartite subgraph. We obtain \(e(H)=O(N^\gamma)\), which is (12). \(\square\)


We now package the two lemmas so that their parameters can be transformed recursively.

Call a bipartite rooted graph \(F\) an \((a,b)\)-model if:

1. its internal set is nonempty and it is \((a,b)\)-balanced;
2. every positive rooted power \(F^{(t)}\) is connected;
3. for every \(t\ge1\),
\[
                   \operatorname{ex}(n,F^{(t)})
                     =O(n^{2-a/b}).                                \tag{19}
\]

An \((a,b)\)-model immediately gives one graph with exponent \(2-a/b\). Indeed, Lemma 1 supplies a \(t\ge1\) for which the reverse estimate
\[
                   n^{2-a/b}=O(\operatorname{ex}(n,F^{(t)}))

after the harmless interpretation of both functions on sufficiently large integers. Property (19) gives the upper estimate for that same \(t\). Thus
\[
                   \operatorname{ex}(n,F^{(t)})
                         =\Theta(n^{2-a/b}).                         \tag{20}
\]
The graph is bipartite because rooted powers preserve bipartiteness.

There is an initial \((1,1)\)-model. Take one internal vertex, one root, and the edge joining them. Its \(t\)-th rooted power is the star \(K_{1,t}\), which is connected. The balance inequality is immediate: the only nonempty internal subset consists of the one internal vertex and has one incident edge. The Kővári–Sós–Turán counting argument gives
\[
                   \operatorname{ex}(n,K_{s,t})=O(n^{2-1/s})

after fixing \(s,t\); for \(s=1\) this is \(O(n)\), exactly (19) with \(a=b=1\). To recall the count, in a \(K_{s,t}\)-free graph the sum over vertices of \(\binom{d(v)}s\) is at most \((t-1)\binom ns\); convexity then bounds the average degree and gives the stated exponent.

Scaling the balance parameters shows that this same graph is an \((a,a)\)-model for every \(a>0\): multiply its balance inequality by \(a\); the exponent remains \(2-a/a=1\).

The crucial closure is the following.


**Lemma 3 (model transformation).** If \(F\) is an \((a,b)\)-model, where \(0<a\le b\), then for every integer \(k\ge0\) there is an
\[
                    (a+kb,\ a+(k+1)b)\text{-model}.                 \tag{21}
\]

**Proof.** First suppose \(k\ge1\). Form \(T_k(F)\), but regard it as a rooted graph in the following way. The old internal vertices remain internal. Each old edge has \(k\) new subdivision vertices. A subdivision vertex is internal if the old edge has at least one internal endpoint; if the old edge joins two roots, promote all its subdivision vertices to roots. The two hubs and all old roots are also roots. This promotion is essential: it makes rooted powers commute with the construction.

Let \(S\) be a set of new internal vertices. Split it into old internal vertices \(S_0\) and subdivision vertices \(S_1\). Let \(I\) be the number of replacement-path edges incident with \(S\). Along a path with \(k\) internal subdivision vertices, two elementary inequalities hold:
\[
 e_F(S_0)+|S_1|\le I,                                               \tag{22}
\]
\[
 (k+1)|S_1|\le kI.                                                  \tag{23}
\]
For (22), an old edge incident with \(S_0\) contributes an end edge of its replacement path, while every chosen subdivision vertex contributes a path edge, with overlaps only improving the inequality. More explicitly, on each path a nonempty set of \(m\) chosen internal positions is incident with at least \(m+1\) path edges; if an endpoint is selected, the corresponding first or last edge is counted. Summing over old edges yields (22). The same observation gives (23): on one path, \(m\le k\) selected internal positions meet at least \(m+1\) edges when \(m>0\), so \((k+1)m\le k(m+1)\); the case \(m=0\) is trivial.

In addition, each old internal vertex in \(S_0\) has its spoke to one hub, and these spokes are distinct from all replacement-path edges. Therefore the number \(e'(S)\) of new graph edges incident with \(S\) satisfies
\[
                         I+|S_0|\le e'(S).                           \tag{24}
\]
The old balance inequality gives
\[
                         b|S_0|\le a e_F(S_0).                      \tag{25}
\]
A linear combination of (22)--(25) now gives
\[
 [a+(k+1)b](|S_0|+|S_1|)
       \le [a+kb]e'(S).                                             \tag{26}
\]
For clarity, one may verify it by replacing \(b|S_0|\) using (25), replacing \((k+1)|S_1|\) using (23), and then using (22) to absorb the resulting \(e_F(S_0)\) and \(|S_1|\) terms into \(I\), after which (24) finishes the estimate. Thus the new rooted graph is balanced with the parameters in (21).

For every \(t\ge1\), its rooted power is naturally isomorphic to
\[
                         T_k(F^{(t)}).                               \tag{27}
\]
To see this, assign each unpromoted subdivision vertex to its layer. A subdivision vertex lying on a root-root edge was promoted, so it is shared among all layers, exactly as the corresponding root-root replacement path in \(T_k(F^{(t)})\). Old vertices and the two hubs plainly correspond. This bijection preserves every spoke and every replacement-path edge.

The graph \(F^{(t)}\) is connected by the model hypothesis and has an edge: balance applied to a singleton internal vertex, together with \(b>0\), forces an incident edge. A proper two-coloring of a graph containing an edge uses both colors. Hence \(T_k(F^{(t)})\), and therefore the new rooted power, is connected.

Apply Lemma 2 to \(F^{(t)}\) with
\[
                         \beta=2-a/b.

a short calculation gives
\[
1+\frac1{k+3-(2-a/b)}
 =1+\frac{b}{a+(k+1)b}
 =2-\frac{a+kb}{a+(k+1)b}.                                        \tag{28}
\]
Together with (27), this proves the required upper estimate for every positive rooted power.

When \(k=0\), use the suspension operation: add the two hubs and the spokes but do not subdivide the old edges, and put both hubs among the roots. The same incident-edge count, now with no subdivision vertices, changes balance from \((a,b)\) to \((a,a+b)\). Rooted powers commute with suspension, and the \(k=0\) instance of the same counting argument changes the exponent from \(2-a/b\) to
\[
1+\frac1{3-(2-a/b)}=2-\frac a{a+b}.

a suspension is connected because one hub reaches the other through any old edge, and every old vertex is adjacent to its corresponding hub. This proves Lemma 3 in all cases. \(\square\)


It remains to prove that the transformations in Lemma 3 generate every pair \((a,b)\) with \(0<a\le b\). We prove this by strong induction on \(b\).

If \(a=b\), use the scaled initial model. Suppose \(a<b\), and put
\[
                         p=b-a.

a simple division step supplies integers \(k,r\ge0\) such that
\[
                         r<p,
 \qquad b+r=(k+2)p.                                                  \tag{29}
\]
Indeed, divide \(b\) by \(p\). If \(p\mid b\), write \(b=qp\). Since \(b>p\), \(q\ge2\); take \(k=q-2\) and \(r=0\). Otherwise write \(b=qp+s\), where \(0<s<p\). Here \(q\ge1\); take
\[
                         k=q-1,
 \qquad r=p-s.

a direct substitution gives (29), and \(0<r<p\).

Since \(p<b\) and \(0<p-r\le p\), the induction hypothesis gives a \((p-r,p)\)-model. Apply Lemma 3 with this model and the integer \(k\) from (29). Its new parameters are
\[
(p-r)+kp,
\qquad
(p-r)+(k+1)p.

after using \(p+a=b\) and (29), these equal \(a\) and \(b\), respectively. Explicitly, (29) says \((k+2)p-r=b=p+a\), whence \((k+1)p-r=a\), which is the first equality; adding \(p\) gives the second. Thus an \((a,b)\)-model exists for every \(0<a\le b\).


We now finish the proof. Let \(\alpha\in\mathbb Q\) satisfy
\[
                         1\le\alpha<2.

after writing
\[
                         2-\alpha=\frac ab

after reduction to positive integers, we have \(a>0\), and \(2-\alpha\le1\) gives \(a\le b\). By the induction just proved, choose an \((a,b)\)-model \(F\). By the realization argument following Lemmas 1 and 2, some positive rooted power \(G=F^{(t)}\) is bipartite and satisfies
\[
\operatorname{ex}(n,G)
  =\Theta\bigl(n^{2-a/b}\bigr)
  =\Theta(n^\alpha).
\]
Finally, \(G\) has a finite vertex set. If it has \(q\) vertices, relabeling its vertices by \(\{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}\) preserves bipartiteness, containment, and every extremal number. We have therefore obtained a bipartite graph on \(q\) vertices whose extremal number is \(\Theta(n^\alpha)\), as required.
